summary: This article explains how a touchscreen senses a finger using tiny electric charges, how it differs from an older pressure-based screen, and how it senses many touches at once.
introduce: Draw two overlapping circles on the board and quickly compare two familiar things, such as a cat and a dog, with the class. Tell students that while reading “How Touchscreens Work” they will look for ways things are alike and different.

keyTerms.def: a thin wire or piece of metal that carries electricity in a device
a small chip inside a device that manages and makes sense of what the device senses
a material that lets electricity pass through it easily

challengeTerms.def: relating to electric charges that are still or built up, rather than flowing as a current
allowing light to pass through so that objects behind it can be seen clearly
to adjust a device carefully so that its readings stay accurate

discussion: Do you agree or disagree that touchscreens are easier to use than buttons? Use evidence from the article to explain.
Explain the difference between how a capacitive touchscreen and an older touchscreen sense a touch.
struggling: Pre-teach electrode, controller, and conductor with pictures or gestures, then let weak readers fill in a T-chart of alike and different with sentence starters.
gifted: Ask strong readers to read a challenging version and write a short paragraph that uses electrostatic, transparent, and calibrate to compare two ideas from the article and explain which difference matters most.
